attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post. The Macdonald quote is context, not the claim.

semantics.note: 'I believe' here is a flat assertion, not a graded hedge. Reading 'effectively every' as almost every company is right. The context defines Uber's experience as rising AI costs that are hard to tie to useful output.

contract.note: Reading 'effectively every' as nearly all, with isolated exceptions allowed, is the ordinary plain reading. The Jan–May 2026 window is reasonable for an ongoing observation published in late May.

evidence.note: ETR surveyed 600 tech leaders in January 2026, and half said AI value outweighs cost. That is a substantial share reporting useful results, not isolated exceptions. The answers are self-reported.

KPMG surveyed 2,145 leaders from Apr 28 to May 25. Only 7% report established ROI and 42% have partial spending visibility, so measurement problems are widespread. It does not show that nearly all lack useful results; some subgroups report meaningful value.

reviews.rationale: The claim says nearly every company shares Uber's experience. In a broad January 2026 survey, about half of respondents said AI value exceeds cost, which meets the contract's contradiction condition. KPMG confirms that measuring ROI is widely hard. But widespread difficulty is not near-universal failure, so it does not rescue the 'effectively every' generalisation. The answers are self-reported, but the contract allows that if it is labelled.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The statement pairs a checkable premise (NVIDIA's revenue depends mostly on three customers) with an evaluative inference (the industry is not healthy; demand is uneven and unsustainable). The proposition captures both.

contract.note: The contract rightly scores the concentration premise and the sustainability inference separately, and separates direct buyers from ultimate demand. 'Healthy' and 'sustainable' have no stated measure, so the result depends on how the inference part is read.

evidence.note: NVIDIA's Q1 FY27 filing gives three direct customers 21%, 17% and 16% of revenue: 54% in total, more than half. It also notes that direct customers resell to indirect ones. It says nothing about whether demand is sustainable.

reviews.rationale: The concentration premise holds: three direct customers supplied 54% of Q1 FY27 revenue. The contract's support condition also needs evidence linking that concentration to unsustainable or unevenly spread ultimate demand, and the packet has none. Nothing meets the contradiction condition either. So the factual premise holds but the claim's core inference is unsettled.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post. The 'Don't worry about the fact that' framing still asserts each item as fact.

semantics.note: The compound proposition keeps all four components and their thresholds (75%+ of compute, >50% of backlog) along with the loaded wording.

contract.note: The contract is reasonable, but several readings are the evaluator's: worldwide operational compute, a combined backlog share across the three providers, a Q1 2026 period, and no stated profit measure. Those choices would decide the result if evidence existed.

evidence.note: A February 2026 tracker forecasts delays for much of the 2026 pipeline. Those are forecasts, not documented failures to finish.
Microsoft's disclosure shows OpenAI driving much of its RPO growth. It covers one provider and gives no customer share, so it cannot test the combined >50% backlog claim.
Anthropic's S-1 shows large net losses, much of them from fair-value changes on convertible notes. It covers one company over a different period and does not show misleading accounting.

reviews.rationale: No evidence in the packet tests the 75% compute share or the >50% combined backlog share. The construction evidence is forecast-based. The profitability evidence covers only Anthropic, over a different period, and does not address the alleged accounting tricks. No component is settled either way.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post. 'I absolutely, 100% believe' is a firm assertion.

semantics.note: This is a firm, high-confidence assertion about present conduct. The proposition drops the 'as a means of expressing growth' motive carried over from the Copilot comparison. That omission is minor and does not change what is testable.

contract.note: Measuring actual inference cost rather than API-equivalent value is fair, because the speaker talks about making inference cheap enough. The April 2026 period and the narrow meaning of 'justify' are the evaluator's choices.

evidence.note: A secondary report of Cursor's estimates of Claude Code compute use in March 2026. It says Anthropic's actual costs are unknown, so it is not verified April cost data.
Altman's January 2025 admission that OpenAI was losing money on Pro. It is from the wrong period and gives no per-user cost.
A June 2026 report values maximum subscription usage at API prices. That is not the providers' actual serving cost, and it covers a different period.

reviews.rationale: The contract needs actual per-subscriber inference costs for both companies in April 2026. The packet has only estimates, API-price valuations, and an admission from an earlier period, none of which show actual serving costs. Nothing establishes or refutes that heavy subscribers cost thousands in real inference expense.
